original_question: Can one construct trial-function and test-function families for Petrov-Galerkin or related spectral methods that are not tailored to only one specific fractional differential equation but instead work across a broad class of problems, still guarantee rapid convergence, possibly yield even faster convergence than current constructions, and admit error analyses in stronger norms such as L^infinity rather than only L^2?
target_in_paper: Sect. 3.2, especially the final paragraph after the worked Petrov–Galerkin example based on the Caputo model problem and the trial/test families generated from the two associated Sturm–Liouville eigenproblems. The exact target is the open research prompt asking for trial and test families usable for a broad class of fractional differential equations, asking whether different basis/test constructions could converge even faster, and noting that the present approach is naturally analyzed in L_2 rather than the stronger L_∞ norm. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft captures the right subsection and nearly all of the substantive content of the paper's open question: it is indeed about Petrov–Galerkin/spectral methods, about avoiding equation-specific trial/test constructions, about retaining rapid convergence over a broader class of fractional problems, about the possibility of even faster convergence from a different basis/test design, and about moving from L_2-based error analysis to the stronger L_∞ norm. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
missing_details: The paper's setting here is numerical solution of fractional ordinary differential equations on a finite interval, within Sect. 3.2 on spectral methods and related techniques; it is not a general question about arbitrary fractional PDEs or all Petrov–Galerkin schemes. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

The specific existing construction being discussed is problem-dependent: from the given differential equation one builds associated Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problems of the first and second kind, and their eigenfunctions become the trial and test functions. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

The nearby worked example is the Caputo initial value problem {}^C D_{-1+}^α y(t)=f(t), y(-1)=y_0 on [-1,1], used only as the simplest illustration of that equation-dependent Petrov–Galerkin construction. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

The paper explicitly includes spectral element methods only by analogy with the spectral construction in Sect. 3.2, so 'related methods' should be kept narrow: spectral or spectral-element methods of that same type. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

What the paper asks for is not merely 'generic basis functions,' but sets of trial and test functions that can be used for a broad class of such differential equations while still guaranteeing rapid convergence of the approximate solutions toward the exact solution. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

The stronger-norm issue is specific: the authors say the present approach naturally leads to convergence/error estimates in L_2 only, whereas other solvers for fractional ordinary differential equations are usually analyzed in L_∞. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

The phrases 'rapid convergence' and 'even faster convergence' are left qualitative in the paper; no explicit rate, asymptotic order, or uniformity statement is specified here. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

The passage is framed as a future research direction/open problem in prose, not as a numbered theorem, conjecture, or equivalence statement with formal hypotheses. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

The paper also notes that the dependence on the precise equation shows up not only in the Sturm–Liouville/basis construction but also in the treatment of a potentially inhomogeneous initial condition, although it says that latter issue can be generalized rather easily. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
refined_question: For spectral or spectral-element Petrov–Galerkin methods for Caputo-type fractional ordinary differential equations on a finite interval, can one construct equation-independent families of trial functions and test functions—rather than families obtained anew from Sturm–Liouville eigenproblems tailored to each given differential equation—that are usable for a broad class of such problems, still guarantee rapid convergence of the approximate solutions to the exact solution, possibly improve the convergence achieved by the currently described construction, and admit convergence/error estimates in the stronger L_∞ norm instead of only in L_2? ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
justification: The draft is clearly targeting the concluding open-problem paragraph of Sect. 3.2. The surrounding context first explains the current equation-dependent Petrov–Galerkin design: generalized-polynomial spectral methods are motivated by endpoint singularities, and for the model Caputo problem on [-1,1] the trial and test spaces are generated from two associated Sturm–Liouville eigenproblems. The authors then state that this strategy depends on the precise form of the differential equation, and immediately formulate the three points your draft paraphrases: broader reusability of trial/test families, possible faster convergence from a different construction, and stronger-norm analysis in L_∞ rather than only L_2. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
